La derivada de un producto <strong>no</s: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Check it with $f=g=x$: $(x\cdot x)' = (x^2)' = 2x$, whereas $1\cdot 1 = 1$. The product rule has those two terms for a reason.
La derivada es, sin discusión, la herram: The derivative is, beyond argument, the most profitable tool at this level, because “rate of change” describes half of reality. In a car, the derivative of position is velocity and the derivative of velocity is acceleration —what the airbag measures to decide whether to fire—. In an epidemic, what the news follows is not the number of infections but its derivative: if the curve “flattens” it means the derivative is falling, even though the total keeps rising. In economics, the marginal cost of making one more unit is a derivative, and setting a price rests on that.
La derivada tiene dos lecturas y las dos: The derivative has two readings and both matter: geometrically it is the gradient of the tangent; physically it is the instantaneous rate of change. If $f$ is position, $f'$ is velocity. If $f$ is the number of infected people, $f'$ is the rate of infection. It is the same mathematical operation.
La idea es la de los engranajes. Si una: The idea is that of gears. If one wheel turns three times as fast as another, and that one turns twice as fast as a third, the first goes six times as fast as the third: the rates multiply. A composed function is exactly that. The inside changes at one rate, the outside reacts at another, and the total rate is the product of the two.
La idea es un truco magnífico. La pendie: The idea is a magnificent trick. The gradient between two points we do know how to compute: it is the gradient of the secant line. If we move the second point towards the first, the secant comes to look more and more like the tangent. And “moving closer in the limit” is exactly what we have known how to do since the previous topic.
La pendiente de la secante tiene nombre: The gradient of the secant has a name of its own, worth knowing because the exam uses it: it is the average rate of change (TVM, from the Spanish) of $f$ on the interval $[a, b]$. It says how much the function changes per unit of $x$, on average, between $a$ and $b$: if $f$ is distance travelled, it is the average speed of the journey; if it is the number of customers, how many come in per hour on average.
La razón se ve con un rectángulo. Imagin: The reason is clear with a rectangle. Imagine one whose sides measure $f$ and $g$ and which is growing with time; its area is $f\cdot g$. If at some instant the side $f$ stretches a little, the area gains a strip of height $g$; if the one that stretches is $g$, it gains a strip of width $f$. The area grows in both places at once, and that is why there are two terms: $f'g$ is what the growth of one side contributes and $fg'$ what the other contributes.

Vale la pena desmontar esa fórmula, porq: It is worth taking that formula apart, because it is more frightening than it should be. The numerator $f(a+h)-f(a)$ is how much the function rises between the two points; the denominator $h$ is how much it runs. Rise over run is the usual gradient, the one for a line. Everything else —the limit— only says what happens when I bring the two points together until they touch.
Y hay que hacerlo con un límite y no sus: And it has to be done with a limit rather than by substituting $h=0$ directly because, if you substitute brutally, you get $\frac{0}{0}$: with no rise and no run there is no gradient to compute. That is exactly the indeterminate form you learned to resolve in the previous topic, and this is why it was needed.
Y hay un uso que te rodea sin que se vea: And there is one use that surrounds you invisibly: finding maxima and minima. Where a function is greatest or least its tangent is flat, that is, its derivative is zero, and that turns “finding the best” into “solving an equation”. A satnav computing the shortest route, an airline allocating seats to maximise revenue, a factory looking for the package that uses least cardboard and even [[ia-que-es|training a model]] all do this same thing: differentiate, set to zero and look. That is the next topic, and the reason this one matters so much.

Ya sabes calcular la pendiente de una re: You already know how to work out the gradient of a line: $m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$. And you know how to resolve the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ by cancelling a factor. The two come together here: a curve does not have one gradient, it has a different one at every point, and to compute it you need a quotient of increments with both increments tending to zero. The derivative is the answer to the question: what is the exact gradient here?
